extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students of topology or real analysis (readers learning topology)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, equivalent criteria, and basic propositions about bases, subspaces, separation axioms (T1, Hausdorff, regular, normal), compactness, local compactness, Lindelöf/σ-compactness, one-point compactification, and product topology. Useful as a reference for proving or verifying these properties for topological spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base for a topology (Proposition 10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family B of subsets of a nonempty set X is a base for some topology T on X iff (a) ⋃B = X, and (b) whenever U and V are in B and x ∈ U ∩ V, there is B in B such that x ∈ B ⊆ U ∩ V. In this case the topology T is the set of all unions of members of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The topology is determined by B. Equivalently, for a given topology T0, B is a base for T0 iff (a) holds and (b0) for each x and each member U of T0 with x ∈ U there exists B∈B with x∈B⊆U. Remark: (b) is satisfied if B is closed under finite intersections; thus any family closed under finite intersections and with union X is a base. Example: in metric spaces the family of open balls is a base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate base criterion for a given topology
rubrics_metrics.description: For a particular given topology T0 on X, a family B is a base for T0 iff (a) X = ⋃B and (b0) for each x and member U of T0 containing x, there is some B∈B such that x∈B⊆U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to check that a proposed subfamily is a base for the already specified topology. Shows relationship between bases and topology they generate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separable (text's usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space (X,T) is said to be separable if it has a base consisting of only countably many sets (text author's convention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes alternate common usage where ‘separable’ means existence of a countable dense set; warns that the countable-base meaning is increasingly common and that the existence of a countable dense set is not particularly useful for general spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative topology / subspace topology
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,T) is a topological space and A ⊆ X is nonempty, the relative topology on A is {U ∩ A : U ∈ T}. The pair (A, T∩A) is called a topological subspace of (X,T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If context permits one may say ‘A is a subspace of X’ when relative topology is understood. Basic checks: unions/intersections behave as expected; the relative topology on B considered as subspace of X equals the relative topology of B considered as subspace of A when B⊆A (Proposition 10.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed sets in a subspace (Proposition 10.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a subspace of X, then the closed sets of A are precisely all sets F∩A where F is closed in X. Consequently B is closed in A iff B = F∩A for some closed F in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for testing closedness in a subspace by lifting to ambient space; used later in proofs about closures and compactness in subspaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction and image continuity (Proposition 10.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:X→Y is continuous and A⊆X, then the restriction f|A:A→Y is continuous at points of A. Also re-defining the codomain to be the image f(X) (i.e., f:X→f(X)) preserves continuity at points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard facts used when working with maps to/from subspaces or considering the image as a subspace of the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation axioms — definitions (T1, Hausdorff, regular, normal)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) T1: every one-point set in X is closed. (ii) Hausdorff (T2): for any two distinct points x and y there exist disjoint open sets U and V with x∈U and y∈V. (iii) Regular: for any point x and any closed set F with x∉F there are disjoint open sets U and V with x∈U and F⊆V. (iv) Normal: for any two disjoint closed subsets E and F there are disjoint open sets U and V with E⊆U and F⊆V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are progressively stronger; Urysohn’s Lemma (later) will connect normality to existence of continuous functions separating closed sets. Examples are provided showing strict separations among these axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent formulations of separation axioms (Proposition 10.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) X is T1 iff for any pair distinct x,y there are open sets separating them in the T1-sense (equivalently each singleton is closed). (b) X is regular iff for any x and closed F with x∉F, there is an open U with x∈U and U_cl ∩ F = ∅ (i.e. U whose closure misses F). (c) X is normal iff for any pair of disjoint closed sets E and F there is an open U with E⊆U and U_cl ∩ F = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These closure-based versions are often handier in proofs (they assert existence of open neighborhoods whose closures are disjoint from the given closed set(s)). The text gives proofs of equivalences and shows how to construct the separating neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications among separation axioms (Proposition 10.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If X is T1 and normal then X is regular. (b) If X is T1 and regular then X is Hausdorff. (c) If X is Hausdorff then X is T1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows logical order and which combinations imply which stronger axioms; proofs use the closure-based formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hausdorff property and uniqueness of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hausdorff property is exactly the right condition to make limits be unique, hence to allow a reasonable notion of convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as motivation: many constructions require Hausdorffness to ensure uniqueness of limits; quotient spaces require care to determine Hausdorffness (later sections give sufficient conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example-use as counterexamples for axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Text supplies explicit examples showing non-implications: spaces that are not T1/regular/normal; T1 but not Hausdorff; Hausdorff but not regular; Hausdorff and regular but not normal; normal but not regular, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate that the axioms are strictly different and provide guidance on constructing spaces used as counterexamples in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity inducing an equivalence relation (Proposition 10.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a regular topological space X define a relation x~y by (text: x is in something c — intended: relation using closures/neighborhoods). Then this relation is an equivalence relation. (Proposition is used as a basis for passing from pseudometric to metric quotients.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how regularity supports passage from pseudometric spaces to metric spaces of equivalence classes; details rely on regularity to get symmetry/transitivity properties. (Text references further development in Section 6.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Local base / first and second countability remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection Ux of open neighborhoods of x is a local base at x if every open set containing x contains some member of Ux. X has a countable local base at each point (first axiom of countability) if for each x such a countable Ux can be chosen; second axiom of countability (text’s separability) means X has a countable base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric spaces have countable local bases given by rational-radius balls. Distinguishes the two countability axioms and their terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open cover, subcover, and Lindelöf space
rubrics_metrics.description: An open cover of X is a collection of open sets whose union is X; an open subcover is a subcollection that still covers. A space X is Lindelöf if every open cover has a countable subcover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relation to separability: every separable X (in the text’s countable-base sense) is Lindelöf. Not every Lindelöf space is separable; an example is constructed in the text (half-open interval topology) to illustrate distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tychonoff’s Lemma / Regular Lindelöf ⇒ normal (Proposition 10.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every regular Lindelöf space is normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: cover each closed set by opens whose closures miss the other closed set, take countable subcovers by Lindelöf property, then thin to disjoint unions to produce disjoint open neighborhoods. Corollary: every regular separable space is normal (Corollary 10.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness — definition and finite-intersection characterization (Proposition 10.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover. Equivalent characterization: X is compact iff every family of closed subsets with the finite-intersection property has nonempty intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite-intersection formulation is frequently more convenient; the equivalence follows by passing to complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous image of compact set is compact (Proposition 10.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f:X→Y is continuous, then f(X) is a compact subset of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate: preimages of an open cover of f(X) give an open cover of X; take finite subcover and push forward. Used to deduce extreme value theorems and more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous real-valued function on compact set attains extrema (Corollary 10.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f:X→R is continuous then f attains its maximum and minimum on X (i.e., f(X) is compact in R and hence closed and bounded, containing its sup and inf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard corollary of continuous image-of-compact and properties of compact subsets of R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subset of compact is compact (Proposition 10.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and E⊆X is closed (in X) then E is compact (with subspace topology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: an open cover of E together with X∖E yields open cover of X; take finite subcover and restrict to E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of compact set and closed set (Lemma 10.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K and E be subsets of X with K compact. If for each x∈K there exist disjoint open sets Ux and Vx with x∈Ux and E⊆Vx, then there exist disjoint open sets U and V such that K⊆U and E⊆V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses compactness to choose a finite subcover from the family {Ux}, then intersect corresponding Vx complements to get the required V. This lemma is a standard tool to separate compact vs closed sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact Hausdorff ⇒ regular and normal (Proposition 10.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every compact Hausdorff space is regular and normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compactness of closed sets and Lemma 10.15 to produce disjoint open neighborhoods; standard structural result about compact Hausdorff spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: In Hausdorff spaces compact sets are closed (Proposition 10.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Hausdorff space every compact subset is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: for x∉K use Hausdorffness to find for each point y∈K disjoint neighborhoods separating x and y; compactness yields finite subcover and shows complement of K is open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous bijection from compact to Hausdorff is a homeomorphism (Corollary 10.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact, Y is Hausdorff, and f:X→Y is continuous, one-to-one, and onto, then f is a homeomorphism (i.e., f^{-1} is continuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: closed sets in X map to compact sets in Y which are closed in Y, so inverse images of closed sets are closed; hence inverse map is continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local compactness and one-point compactification (definitions and Proposition 10.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: X is locally compact if every point has a compact neighborhood. The one-point compactification X* = X ∪ {∞} has topology T* consisting of open sets of X plus sets whose complements in X are closed compact subsets. Proposition 10.19: (X*,T*) is compact, X is open in X*, and the relative topology on X is the original topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one-point compactification of R is topologically a circle, of R^2 a sphere. Construction is used to connect local compactness to compact Hausdorff spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of when one-point compactification is Hausdorff (Proposition 10.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: X* (one-point compactification) is Hausdorff iff X is both locally compact and Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward direction: if X* is Hausdorff then X being a subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff, and near each point one can separate from ∞ to get compact neighborhoods, so X is locally compact. Converse: if X is locally compact Hausdorff then complements of compact neighborhoods provide basic neighborhoods of ∞ and separate points, making X* Hausdorff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally compact Hausdorff ⇒ regular (Corollary 10.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every locally compact Hausdorff space is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: form X*, the one-point compactification, which is compact Hausdorff hence regular; then subspace inherits regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of compact and closed sets in locally compact Hausdorff spaces (Corollary 10.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K and F are disjoint closed sets in a locally compact Hausdorff space and K is compact, then there exist disjoint open sets U and V with K⊆U and F⊆V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of Lemma 10.15 plus local compactness and regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of compact neighborhood with compact closure (Corollary 10.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is compact in a locally compact Hausdorff space, then there exists a compact set L with K⊆L° (i.e., K is contained in the interior of some compact L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses one-point compactification and regularity of the compactified space to find open U with K⊆U and U_cl compact; take L = U_cl.

rubrics_metrics.name: σ-compact definition and equivalence with Lindelöf for locally compact spaces (Proposition 10.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: X is σ-compact if it is a countable union of compact sets. In a locally compact space, X is σ-compact iff X is Lindelöf. Consequently every σ-compact locally compact Hausdorff space is normal (via regular + Lindelöf ⇒ normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs the countable union by taking interiors of compact neighborhoods and using Lindelöf property; conversely σ-compact gives countable covers of compacts and hence Lindelöf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing exhaustion by compact sets in σ-compact locally compact spaces (Proposition 10.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is σ-compact and locally compact Hausdorff then there exists an increasing sequence K1 ⊆ K2 ⊆ ... of compact sets with ⋃Kn = X and Kn ⊆ (Kn+1)° for all n (i.e., each Kn is contained in interior of next).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful technical tool for constructing partitions of unity and for proofs requiring exhaustion of X by compact subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product topology: definition and basic base description
rubrics_metrics.description: Given spaces {Xs}s∈S, the product X=∏s∈S Xs is given the weakest topology making each projection ps:X→Xs continuous. A base for the product topology consists of finite intersections of inverse images of opens: sets of the form ⋂_{k=1}^n p_{s_k}^{-1}(U_{s_k}) (equivalently boxes U_{s_1}×...×U_{s_n}×∏_{s∉{s_k}} Xs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: basic open sets impose constraints at only finitely many coordinates. For sequences (countable product) basic opens restrict finitely many coordinates. Important distinction: finite intersections suffice; infinite intersections need not be open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff (Proposition 10.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: The topological product of Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff: if f and g are distinct elements of the product, they differ at some coordinate s; separate their coordinates in Xs by disjoint opens and pull back to get disjoint opens in the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard coordinatewise argument using continuity of projection maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tychonoff Product Theorem (Theorem 10.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: The topological product of compact topological spaces is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated here as the central compactness result for products (proof and consequences developed in following sections). This is the general Tychonoff theorem (equivalent to the Axiom of Choice in set-theoretic strength).
